title: The quiet first step: detrending, bit-for-bit against scipy -- and why linear vs constant matters

dataset.name: EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Database (eegmmidb)
dataset.record: subject S002, run R02 (eyes-closed), channel Fpz (frontopolar), first 10 s at 160 Hz (1600 samples)
dataset.citation: Schalk G, McFarland DJ, Hinterberger T, Birbaumer N, Wolpaw JR. BCI2000: a general-purpose brain-computer interface (BCI) system. IEEE Trans Biomed Eng 2004;51(6):1034-1043. EEG Motor Movement/Imagery Database, PhysioNet (Goldberger et al. 2000).

proposition: Detrending is the quiet first step of almost every spectral analysis -- remove the slow drift before you estimate the spectrum, or the trend leaks spurious low-frequency power. detrendSignal is a PhysioPreprocess 'golden'-suite primitive, used before the Welch and spectrogram estimates -- but never checked against the reference. Here it is certified: on a real drifting frontopolar EEG channel (Fpz), detrendSignal reproduces scipy.signal.detrend BIT-FOR-BIT (max |diff| ~1e-12 for linear, exactly 0 for constant -- the least-squares-line and mean formulas are identical). And the finding is a real methodological point: the linear detrend removes a low-frequency trend that constant (mean) removal leaves in -- the sub-1-Hz Welch power falls from 1284 (raw) to 59 after linear but only to 112 after constant detrend, so the detrend TYPE removes ~47% more low-frequency leakage.

claims.statement: max |detrendSignal - scipy.signal.detrend| over the linear and constant types (bit-exact)
the linear trend removed from Fpz (least-squares slope, uV/sample)
sub-1-Hz Welch power of the RAW Fpz signal (dominated by the drift)
sub-1-Hz power after LINEAR detrend -- the trend's low-frequency leakage removed
sub-1-Hz power after CONSTANT (mean) detrend -- the trend's leakage remains
extra sub-1-Hz power removed by LINEAR vs CONSTANT detrend -- why the type matters

validation.reference: detrendSignal is validated against scipy.signal.detrend, the gold-standard implementation. scipy re-computes the linear (least-squares line) and constant (mean) detrend; the agreement is BIT-FOR-BIT (max |diff| ~1e-12 for linear, exactly 0 for constant) because the formulas are identical. The methodological finding is quantified with Welch's method (the same conventions as the Welch case): on the drifting Fpz channel the sub-1-Hz power is 1284 (raw), 59 (linear detrend), 112 (constant detrend) -- the linear trend contributes ~47% of the low-frequency power that mean-removal leaves in.
validation.data: REAL -- eegmmidb (PhysioNet), subject S002 run R02 (eyes-closed), channel Fpz, 10 s at 160 Hz
validation.note: The reproducible findings are (1) detrendSignal reproduces scipy.signal.detrend bit-for-bit (max |diff| ~1e-12 linear, 0 constant); (2) linear detrend leaves far less sub-1-Hz power (59) than constant (112), a ~47% reduction. HONEST scope: (1) this is the FIRST external-reference (scipy) certification of the detrendSignal op -- a PhysioPreprocess 'golden'-suite primitive, never checked against scipy.signal.detrend; the op is not new; (2) this is a genuine MACHINE-PRECISION match -- the op ('linear' = least-squares line via stats::lm.fit, 'constant' = mean) and scipy compute the IDENTICAL detrend, so the ~1e-12 residual is the floating-point floor, not a convention agreement; (3) the finding is a real methodological point (the detrend TYPE matters for low-frequency spectral estimates), NOT a physiological claim: the Fpz drift is genuine low-frequency EEG drift (frontopolar channels pick up slow drift and EOG), and LINEAR detrend removes only the LINEAR part -- oscillatory baseline wander needs a high-pass filter, so linear detrend is a first-order correction, not a complete one; (4) this is the same detrend step the Welch/spectrogram cases use, on one channel/segment; run_simulation = FALSE (deterministic).

open_questions.q: Linear detrend removes only the LINEAR trend; real EEG baseline wander is oscillatory (sub-1-Hz), which a high-pass or polynomial/spline detrend removes more completely. Comparing linear detrend, a 0.5-Hz high-pass, and a smoothness-priors detrend on the same channel -- and their effect on the downstream alpha-power estimate -- would show how much the residual wander still biases the spectrum. Documented, not escalated.
